title: Order in transition: The British energy-core and early capitalist technique
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Technion-Israel Institute of Technology - Faculty of Architecture and Town Planning and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Order in transition: The British energy-core and early capitalist technique

affiliations.org_name: Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN
Technion-Israel Institute of Technology - Faculty of Architecture and Town Planning
Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.abstract: How did the energy transition to fossil fuels consolidate the business power of British energy firms between 1870 and 1914? We show that the rise of British industry’s energy-core — energy-intensive industries and fuel providers — rested on controlling transitional processes through novel price-making practices that later became central to twentieth-century capitalism.,During the nineteenth century, developments in energy use and conversion efficiency were accompanied by increased industrial output and productivity. However, employing a Capital as Power approach, we argue that only during the 1890s — the ”seven good years” (1894–1900) — when the energy-core first endeavored to control differential prices, were these developments realized as differential accumulation.,By presenting novel conceptual tools and empirical findings, we trace how the transition to fossil fuels catalyzed the development of capitalist power mechanisms that shape and restrict transitional processes past and present.

title: Are stated preference valuation methods fit for purpose in a pluralist world? Using hybrid choice experiments to link value pluralism to preferences for nature restoration
affiliations: University of Copenhagen, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of Copenhagen

detail.title: Are stated preference valuation methods fit for purpose in a pluralist world? Using hybrid choice experiments to link value pluralism to preferences for nature restoration

affiliations.org_name: University of Copenhagen
Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN
Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN
University of Copenhagen

detail.abstract: Economic valuation is being critiqued for a lack of ability to capture a plurality of values of nature. For the legitimacy of economic valuation methods as a decision support tool, it is important to understand how people holding different values for nature engage with stated valuation of nature. Using a latent class hybrid choice modelling approach, we link responses to the Plural Values of Nature scale to choice experiment data on nature restoration from Poland, Slovakia and the Netherlands. In this manner, we provide empirical evidence that stated valuation methods can capture general preferences of people holding a plurality of values, while finding empirical constraints in the elicitation of monetary values from people holding strong intrinsic or relational values. All groups conduct trade-offs, thereby rejecting lexicographic preferences, although we do find evidence of non-attendance to cost for people holding strong intrinsic or relational values. These groups highly skew mean value estimates and hold a specific configuration of preferences, highlighting the essential need to identify and address their preferences if representativeness is sought. Further, we show that common socio-economic covariates relate to WTP mainly through values of nature as a mediator rather than directly. We demonstrate that people holding strong intrinsic value of nature are more likely to support nature restoration, whereas opposition aligns with instrumental values. Relational values matter in Poland but not in the other two countries. This indicates that in our search for understanding heterogeneity in value assessment, we need to look beyond measurable socio-economic characteristics.

title: Climate Policy Support and the Untapped Potential of the Post-Growth Framework: Representative Survey Evidence from Germany
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and German Institute of Development and Sustainability (IDOS)

detail.title: Climate Policy Support and the Untapped Potential of the Post-Growth Framework: Representative Survey Evidence from Germany

affiliations.org_name: Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN
German Institute of Development and Sustainability (IDOS)

detail.abstract: Public support is key for implementing urgently needed socio-ecological transitions, including climate policies. To achieve such transitions, post-growth concepts as alternatives to growth-based models have seen increasing support among academics and activists. However, important gaps remain. In the first place, less is known about citizens’ support for post-growth. In parallel, evidence is needed on whether public support for climate policies can increase by linking them to a broader socio-economic transition following post-growth approaches. Using nationally representative survey data collected from German citizens, first, we show that citizens’ views on economic growth are more nuanced than a simple trade-off between growth and environmental protection. We also shed light on an important but under-explored dimension of post-growth: the aspect of global fairness and responsibility. We find that it is particularly this component of post-growth that people support. Second, by linking post-growth to specific climate policy instruments (the energy transition including the coal exit) currently implemented in Germany, we find that those people in support of post-growth also exhibit higher support for the energy transition. In addition, a key result of this study is the potential of increasing overall public support for climate policies by implementing it within a post-growth framework, i.e. combining it with more structural socio-economic policy instruments. We investigate in particular the crucial role of (economic) concerns for policy support.

title: Ambient Temperature and Emergency Department Visits: Association and Short-Term Prediction

detail.title: Ambient Temperature and Emergency Department Visits: Association and Short-Term Prediction

affiliations.org_name: Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN
Indus Hospital & Health Network
National University of Sciences & Technology (NUST), Islamabad, Pakistan
Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN
Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN
Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN
Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.abstract: Extreme and changing environmental conditions can influence emergency healthcare demand, making the ability to understand and anticipate ED utilization a global public health priority. However, evidence on temperature related ED utilization and short-term forecasting remains limited in low- and middle-income settings, particularly in South Asia. We examined the associa tion between ambient temperature and daily adult emergency department (ED) visits and evaluated meteorological and historical demand variables for short-term ED forecasting in Karachi, Pakistan. We conducted a retrospective time-series study of 1,322,537 adult ED visits recorded at Indus Hospital and Health Network over a 10-year period (2016–2025). Lagged Pearson correlations were used to assess associations between meteorological variables and ED visits, followed by a quasi-Poisson distributed lag non-linear model (DLNM) to characterize nonlinear and delayed temperature effects. SARIMA, SARIMAX, XGBoost, and LightGBM were trained using temporally or dered data and evaluated on an unseen test period. Temperature showed the strongest correlation with ED visits among the evaluated meteorological variables. Using 28.3◦C as the reference, cumulative RR was 0.839 (95% CI 0.792–0.889) at 18.5◦C and 1.062 (95% CI 1.034–1.091) at 31.7◦C, demon strating a nonlinear temperature-associated pattern. For forecasting, models incorporated meteorological conditions, calendar variables, and historical ED demand. LightGBM achieved an MAPE of 6.55% and R2 of 0.56, followed by XGBoost (6.63%; R2 0.54). SHAP analysis showed that recent ED demand, particularly the seven-day rolling mean and recent lags, contributed most to predictions. This large, decade-long dataset provides evidence from a resource-constrained setting and demonstrates the potential of integrating en vironmental and demand signals to support short-term emergency healthcare planning under changing climatic conditions.

title: Robust Portfolio Choice under Business-Cycle Ambiguity
affiliations: University of Shanghai for Science and Technology - Business School, Wuhan University and South China Normal University

detail.title: Robust Portfolio Choice under Business-Cycle Ambiguity

affiliations.org_name: University of Shanghai for Science and Technology - Business School
Wuhan University
South China Normal University

detail.abstract: This paper studies robust consumption and portfolio choice under ambiguity regarding diffusion, disaster jump, and business-cycle transition risks in complete and incomplete markets. With CRRA preferences, we derive semi-analytical optimal policies and quantify welfare costs. Market completeness changes how ambiguity aversion is transmitted into portfolio choice. In complete markets, ambiguity aversion toward a particular risk operates primarily through the corresponding exposure, with small cross-risk effects. In incomplete markets, ambiguity aversion is jointly transmitted through the stock position, with predominantly own-regime and small cross-regime effects. Business-cycle transition ambiguity aversion exhibits directional asymmetry, with normal-to-crisis ambiguity aversion generating larger policy and welfare effects than the reverse. Market completeness also changes the relative welfare importance of ambiguity aversion. Normal-to-crisis transition ambiguity aversion has the largest effect in complete markets, whereas diffusion-risk ambiguity aversion generally dominates in incomplete markets. Overall, the economic consequences of business-cycle ambiguity depend critically on transition direction and market completeness.

title: The Ukrainian Lab: Post-War Reconstruction of Central and Eastern Europe Through Praxeology and Radical Deregulation

detail.title: The Ukrainian Lab: Post-War Reconstruction of Central and Eastern Europe Through Praxeology and Radical Deregulation

affiliations.org_name: Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.abstract:
Background. The emerging donor consensus on Ukraine's post-war reconstruction rests on centralized administrative planning and external financial aid. From the perspective of the Austrian School of Economics (L. von Mises, F. Hayek), this blueprint reproduces the economic calculation problem, erroneously treating reconstruction as an engineering problem of capital allocation rather than a discovery problem of market processes.

Objective. To substantiate an alternative institutional model for Ukraine's post-war reconstruction, conceptualizing Ukraine not as a passive recipient of aid, but as a market laboratory and an institutional vanguard for the Central and Eastern European (CEE) region through praxeology and radical deregulation.

Methods. The study employs praxeological analysis, institutional comparison, and an empirical case study of the Ukrainian defense-technology (Defense Tech) sector during 2022–2025.

Results. The paper demonstrates that centralized concessional financing severs the link between capital allocation and entrepreneurial risk appraisal, while rigid regulatory harmonization imposes premature compliance costs. Conversely, the Ukrainian defense-technology sector serves as a stark empirical confirmation of Hayek's discovery procedure and Kirznerian entrepreneurial alertness. By 2025, approximately 500 private manufacturers operated in the sector, with only ~100 holding state contracts. Decentralized trial-and-error mechanisms increased strike accuracy from ~30% in 2022 to ~70% two years later, driving sectoral revenues to 100 billion UAH in 2024. Based on these findings, three core institutional pillars are proposed: 1) absolute inviolability of private property rights against oligarchic capture and state expropriation; 2) proactive radical deregulation (flat-tax structure, removal of licensing barriers, flexible labor markets); and 3) quasi-constitutional fiscal rules capping discretionary state spending.

Practical Value. The proposed framework reinterprets Ukraine's current lack of deep regulatory sedimentation as a unique comparative advantage. By establishing a minimal, highly protective legal state, Ukraine can shift from trailing the CEE average to leading an alternative, highly dynamic regional development trajectory.

title: The Law of Prediction
affiliations: University of California, Irvine School of Law

detail.title: The Law of Prediction

affiliations.org_name: University of California, Irvine - School of Law

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are “prediction machines.” They are being used to predict recidivism, creditworthiness, honesty, and fraud, often causing harm to the marginalized and vulnerable. Legal scholars tend to see these technologies and their harms as exceptional and new. But prediction is nothing new for law. AI is merely the latest instantiation of the social practice of prediction, a practice that the law has long helped define, normalize, and embed into society. Law has built both doctrine and procedures to calibrate prediction practices—to sort the beneficial uses of prediction from the harmful, to govern the line between them, and to decide who gets to draw it. This Article uses case studies in the law to excavate that history with the goal of informing timely debates about public and private uses of prediction.

In so doing, this Article makes three contributions to legal scholarship. The first contribution is conceptual. The Article demystifies AI by reducing it to its predictive core and argues that prediction is a social practice co-constructed by law. Using case studies in which various areas of law rely on criminal records, earning histories, and financial information to make predictions about the future behavior of individuals, the Article then makes its descriptive contribution. It demonstrates that the law constructs prediction as a dilemma between knowledge production for predictors and threats to liberal principles of dignity and due process for those subject to prediction. The Article then provides a novel taxonomy of the law’s policy responses to this predictive dilemma. The third contribution is normative. The Article applies these lessons to the AI context, offering two imaginaries of AI policy—namely, one based on applying the law’s traditional approach to prediction and another based on anti-subordination principles. Both approaches would re-imagine ongoing debates about how best to regulate AI at the policy level and how judges, juries, and advocates should address AI predictions in their cases.

title: Is More Always Better? The Differential Effects of Clip Quantity and Account Breadth on Sales in Live-Streaming Commerce
affiliations: Guangdong University of Technology - School of Management, Guangdong University of Foreign Studies, University of Pittsburgh and Guangdong University of Foreign Studies

detail.title: Is More Always Better? The Differential Effects of Clip Quantity and Account Breadth on Sales in Live-Streaming Commerce

affiliations.org_name: Guangdong University of Technology - School of Management
Guangdong University of Foreign Studies
University of Pittsburgh
Guangdong University of Foreign Studies

detail.abstract: Live-streaming clips have emerged as an important content format in live-streaming commerce, enabling streamers and merchants to extend content reach beyond the focal broadcast. However, whether greater clip operations always improve sales performance remains unclear. Drawing on the mere exposure effect and signaling theory, this study conceptualizes live-streaming clip operations along two dimensions: clip quantity and clip account breadth. Using a streamer-session panel dataset from Douyin, we examine their dynamic effects on live-streaming sales volume, the moderating role of authorization, contextual heterogeneity, and their incremental predictive value beyond routine live-stream features. The results show that streamers adopting clip strategies achieve higher sales volume than those without clip operations. More importantly, the two dimensions exhibit distinct temporal effects. Clip quantity generates positive sales effects that emerge primarily in the subsequent live session, whereas clip account breadth produces a delayed negative effect. Authorization further strengthens the delayed negative effect of clip account breadth but does not enhance the positive effect of clip quantity. Additional analyses show that the negative effect of clip account breadth is stronger in highly interactive and long-engagement sessions, whereas the benefit of clip quantity emerges earlier when more products are presented. Further analyses through Machine-learning demonstrate that clip characteristics provide incremental predictive information beyond routine live-stream metrics. By revealing the contrasting effects of exposure intensity and dissemination-source breadth, this study extends research on derivative content in live-streaming commerce and offers practical guidance for managing clip operations and multi-account dissemination strategies.

title: The Asymmetric Conversion of Digital Time: Temporal Affordance Architecture in Video Games
affiliations: The Open University and The Open University

detail.title: The Asymmetric Conversion of Digital Time: Temporal Affordance Architecture in Video Games

affiliations.org_name: The Open University
The Open University

detail.abstract: Digital games are played over time, but game length, replayability and price are often studied separately from market reach and review evaluations. This study develops the concept of temporal affordance architecture to examine how completion, optional play beyond the main story, recurrence, and price relative to expected playtime relate to market visibility and aggregate review positivity. We combine two public, title-level datasets and use descriptive analyses, OLS models with HC3 standard errors, spline models of recurrence, and an exploratory five-profile k-means analysis. Completion and extension are positively associated with review volume and estimated ownership, but show little association with review positivity. Fitted recurrence curves peak at a lower level for positivity than for review visibility and ownership reach. Absolute price is positively associated with visibility, while price per main-story hour is negatively associated with it. Overall, the results suggest that temporal features relate differently to market reach and aggregate evaluation.

title: Hot criticism, cool praise: The interplay between contrastive eWOM and emotional intensity in shaping consumers’ eWOM retransmission intention
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Hot criticism, cool praise: The interplay between contrastive eWOM and emotional intensity in shaping consumers’ eWOM retransmission intention

affiliations.org_name: Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN
Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN
Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN
Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.abstract: AbstractPurpose: Drawing on Cognitive-Affective Personality System (CAPS) theory, this study examines how contrastive eWOM (negative contrast vs. positive contrast) and eWOM emotional intensity (low vs. high) interact to influence consumers’ eWOM retransmission intention. It further investigates emotional arousal and perceived diagnosticity as dual psychological mechanisms and eWOM channel (weak-tie vs. strong-tie) as a boundary condition.Design/methodology/approach: Three online scenario-based experiments test the proposed hypotheses. Study 1 manipulated contrastive eWOM and emotional intensity to examine their interactive effect on eWOM retransmission intention. Study 2 replicates this interaction in a different product context, tests the mediating roles of emotional arousal and perceived diagnosticity, and rules out processing fluency and self-presentation motivation. Study 3 examines whether eWOM channel (weak-tie vs. strong-tie) moderates the two psychological pathways.Findings: For negative-contrast eWOM, high emotional intensity generates stronger retransmission intention than low emotional intensity, primarily through emotional arousal. For positive-contrast eWOM, low emotional intensity generates stronger retransmission intention than high emotional intensity, primarily through perceived diagnosticity. Moreover, strong-tie (vs. weak-tie) channels amplify the arousal pathway of high-intensity negative-contrast eWOM, whereas weak-tie (vs. strong-tie) channels strengthen the diagnosticity pathway of low-intensity positive-contrast eWOM.Originality/value: This study incorporates the directional incongruence between consumers’ pre-existing brand attitudes and external eWOM valence into eWOM communication research, explaining when emotional intensity facilitates or inhibits eWOM retransmission. The findings also provide theoretical grounding and practical implications for brand crisis communication, brand-image recovery, and multichannel content allocation.

title: Unilateral Incentives and Informative Experimentationin Cournot Learning

detail.title: Unilateral Incentives and Informative Experimentationin Cournot Learning

affiliations.org_name: King Saud University

detail.abstract: Firms facing unknown demand must infer the effect of a unilateral quantity change from observations generated while their rivals also adjust. We study this problem in Cournot games with a strongly monotone negative marginal-profit map and noisy price signals. For demand that is affine in an unknown parameter, we characterize identification of unilateral incentives and distinguish it from identification of the parameter and the Nash equilibrium. Observationally equivalent demand models can have different equilibria, so repeated observations need not support competitive learning. Under Gaussian noise, sequential information bounds quantify this obstruction. We then analyze a decentralized payoff-based procedure with vanishing quantity experiments and covariance correction. Suitable experiment amplitudes and step sizes ensure almost-sure convergence of played quantities to Nash, including boundary equilibria. In a linear duopoly, uncorrected common experiments instead converge to the joint-profit maximizer because the estimated incentives include rivals' simultaneous movements. For a fixed-baseline observation stage, we derive the exact minimum weighted perturbation cost of prescribed information under amplitude constraints, together with lower and upper bounds for competitive implementation. Numerical experiments with curved demand and unequal costs separate the common-experiment limit from both Nash and joint-profit maximization. They also examine increasing experiment correlation, for which we obtain a sufficient convergence condition in the nonlinear example. The results distinguish informative variation, accumulated information, and the learning rule that uses it; profits above Nash alone do not identify collusion.
